stem: A per-step fit assessment finds eight of nine workflow steps high-volume and machine-readable; the ninth is a loan-denial decision regulation requires a licensed credit officer to make. A 200-person servicing team wants one verdict. What should happen to that step?

opts.t: Automate the denial decision outright, since the step is high-volume and machine-readable like the rest of the workflow.
The credit officer makes the decision; the model prepares a complete draft recommendation and supporting evidence for review.
Automate the decision, tracking the override rate as a proxy signal for the delayed outcome.
Automate the denial decision fully, adding a confidence threshold so only low-confidence cases route to the credit officer.

whyRight: Regulation requires a licensed decision-maker for this step, so the model cannot make the call regardless of accuracy. Preparing a complete draft recommendation captures nearly all the cycle-time value while leaving the statutory decision itself with the credit officer, satisfying the regulatory boundary.

whyWrong.A: This discards the stated regulatory requirement entirely; a licensed decision-maker must make the call no matter how strong the step's volume and machine-readability fit signals are.
whyWrong.C: The proxy-signal fix addresses feedback that arrives too late to steer design, a different problem; it does nothing to satisfy a statutory human-decision-maker requirement.
whyWrong.D: A confidence threshold is a monitoring mechanism, not a decision-maker; no threshold level substitutes for the licensed sign-off the regulation states the step requires.

t1Clause: regulation requires a licensed credit officer to make

stem: A claims operations lead proposes shipping a triage assistant now and comparing before/after metrics once dashboards are live, since no handling-time data exists for the current 1,200-case monthly queue. Should the team proceed before instrumenting a baseline?

opts.t: Approve the plan; derive the baseline retrospectively from the new system's own dashboards once it ships.
Survey claims staff on whether the process feels slow, and use that sentiment as the comparison baseline.
Argue the assistant's value as a new capability instead, since transformation claims need no per-unit efficiency baseline.
Reject the proposal; measure current handling time before shipping, so the launch has a real before-value to compare against.

whyRight: The proposal has no before-value to compare against, so any post-launch number is uninterpretable. Measuring current handling time first, before shipping, gives the launch a real baseline, turning the eventual comparison into evidence rather than an unsupported claim of improvement.

whyWrong.A: Deriving a baseline from the new system's own logs only captures what the new system chose to record, after the change already happened; it cannot recover the process it replaced.
whyWrong.B: Sentiment about whether a process feels slow is not the unit the business case is written in; the requirement is a measurable before, not a qualitative impression.
whyWrong.C: This applies only when no prior process exists; here a 1,200-case monthly queue is already running, so an efficiency baseline is the right frame, not an exemption.

stem: A 40-person support organization's audit rated 92% of model responses fully correct; reviewers still hand-edit the rest before sending, and those edits are discarded, not recorded. Leadership proposes a real-time accuracy dashboard. Does it close the loop?

opts.t: No; capture the discarded edits as labelled events and route the disagreement cases into the evaluation set and prompt revisions.
No; replace the model with a higher-accuracy version, since the correction rate shows the current model is not good enough.
Yes; the real-time dashboard tracking accuracy and volume trends over time is sufficient to close the loop on its own.
No; route the discrepancy signal to the retrieval and indexing layer so future responses cite corrected sources.

whyRight: The dashboard only measures the plateau; it carries no correctness label. The reviewers' hand-edits already contain that label, the gap between what the model produced and what was actually sent. Capturing those edits as events and routing them into the eval set and prompts is what changes behaviour.

whyWrong.B: The audit already rated 92% of responses fully correct, so a capability ceiling is not the binding constraint; the discarded edits, not model accuracy, are the missing signal.
whyWrong.C: A dashboard records what happened without a correctness label attached; it can show the plateau but cannot itself supply the signal that would end it.
whyWrong.D: Nothing in the scenario points to a citation or retrieval failure; the edits being discarded are general correctness corrections, not source-attribution errors the indexing layer would fix.

t1Clause: reviewers still hand-edit the rest before sending

stem: A support workflow uses a drafting role and a review role that can only start once a draft exists; the review role's confidential notes must not enter the drafting context. Which two facts justify multiple agents' added token cost? Select two.

opts.t: Isolating the review role's confidential notes from the drafting role's context is a valid justification.
Restricting each role to only the access its task requires is a valid justification.
Splitting the work across agents is a more sophisticated design regardless of the access constraints.
Splitting drafting and review into separate agents parallelizes the work and reduces wall-clock turnaround time.

whyRight: Both facts are independently stated: the confidential review notes must stay out of the drafting context (isolation), and each role is restricted to only the access its task needs (privilege separation). Either alone funds the added token cost; here both apply, so multi-agent is justified twice over.

whyWrong.C: Splitting roles is not justified by sophistication; the design earns its token cost only through a stated isolation or privilege requirement, both of which are present here for other reasons.
whyWrong.D: Review is gated on a draft existing first, so the two roles run sequentially; parallelizing only becomes possible if that dependency is removed, which is not the case here.

t1Clause: that can only start once a draft exists

stem: A document-intake pipeline forwards uploaded files directly to the model for summarization; some contain Social Security numbers, and a compliance officer requires raw identifiers never reach the model. What should the boundary do before the model call?

opts.t: Forward files to the model as-is, and log an alert whenever a Social Security number appears in the output.
Let files reach the model unchanged, and scrub Social Security numbers from the model's response before it is returned.
Redact Social Security numbers from each file at the input boundary before any file reaches the model.
Reject only the files where a Social Security number is detected, and forward the rest unchanged to the model.

whyRight: Post-model filtering cannot undo an identifier the model already processed; redaction has to happen before the model call. Handling it at the input boundary, rather than downstream, is the only point that prevents the exposure rather than merely detecting or repairing it afterward.

whyWrong.A: Logging an alert after the number appears in the output confirms the exposure already happened; the compliance requirement is that the identifier never reaches the model in the first place.
whyWrong.B: Scrubbing the response after the fact does not undo the exposure; the model has already processed the raw identifier by the time its output is edited.
whyWrong.D: Rejecting the whole file discards the summary the requirement still needs; redacting just the identifier satisfies the constraint without losing the rest of the content.

stem: A claims-status lookup follows the same three fixed steps every time — verify the claim ID, pull the current policy record, report status — but the record changes daily and must be current for a 5,000-employee benefits desk. Which rung fits?

opts.t: Use an agent, since each request's handling path cannot be predicted in advance.
Keep the fixed three-step sequence, and retrieve the current policy record at that step so the answer reflects today's data.
Keep the fixed three-step sequence exactly as it runs today, without changing how the policy record is retrieved.
Add a verification layer that cross-checks the record against a monitoring dashboard before reporting the claim status.

whyRight: The three-step path is enumerable and unchanging, so it belongs in code, not agentic control-flow. The only unmet requirement is data currency, which retrieval solves directly at the relevant step, augmenting the fixed workflow without introducing the nondeterminism a path change would require.

whyWrong.A: The stem states the three steps run in the same order every time; that is exactly the enumerable path an agent's non-enumerability justification requires and does not have here.
whyWrong.C: This preserves the right rung but leaves the actual problem untouched: the policy record still would not be current unless the retrieval step is added.
whyWrong.D: A verification and monitoring layer confirms whether the record was current after the fact; it does not make the workflow retrieve current data in the first place.

t1Clause: follows the same three fixed steps every time

stem: An operations lead wants to replace a five-step intake pipeline with an agent, calling it rigid. The pipeline still extracts five fixed fields from about 500 weekly submissions, always in the same order. What is the correct architecture?

opts.t: Keep the fixed pipeline; nothing in the requirements makes the field set or step order unknown in advance.
Switch to an agent with dynamic adaptive planning so it can map each submission's structure as it goes.
Keep the pipeline, but add an agentic fallback branch triggered whenever a submission takes longer than usual to process.
Adopt the agent, and require a senior engineer to sign off on each run before it proceeds.

whyRight: Nothing in the requirements makes the field set, count, or order unknown in advance; the pipeline is fully enumerable at real volume. Feeling rigid is a stated preference, not a non-enumerable requirement, so the fixed pipeline is the correct, cheaper rung and the agent proposal should be rejected.

whyWrong.B: Dynamic adaptive planning is bought by a non-enumerable path; here every field, order, and step is already known, so the planning capability pays for nothing the task needs.
whyWrong.C: Runtime speed is not what makes a path enumerable or not; branching on how long a submission takes adds nondeterminism the fixed field set never required.
whyWrong.D: Sign-off adds a human gate to a design that has not been decided yet; it does not settle whether an agent is warranted, only supervises one that isn't.

t1Clause: The pipeline still extracts five fixed fields from about 500 weekly submissions, always in the same order

stem: Two of five configured sources fail to return data before a subagent's deadline in a multi-agent synthesis pipeline; the coordinator must produce one report for a client-facing summary due today. How should synthesis proceed with the incomplete input set?

opts.t: Re-delegate queries to the two failed sources and wait for them to return before synthesising.
Pause the report and escalate to a human until all five sources return successfully.
Compile the report from the three returned sources and present it as complete, without noting the two missing.
Synthesise from the three returned sources, marking which claims are well-supported and which lack coverage.

whyRight: Two of five sources failing to return is a genuine access failure, not a quality gap a re-query would fix, and the deadline requires proceeding. Marking which claims are well-supported versus missing lets the report degrade gracefully instead of stalling or silently overstating its own coverage.

whyWrong.A: Re-delegating targets a coverage gap caused by inadequate querying with sources available; here the sources themselves failed to return, so retrying risks missing the deadline for no gain.
whyWrong.B: Waiting for all five sources abandons the same-day deadline the coordinator is required to meet, in pursuit of completeness the scenario does not require.
whyWrong.C: Presenting the report as complete without noting the two missing sources hides exactly the coverage gap a client-facing summary needs disclosed.

t1Clause: Two of five configured sources fail to return data before a subagent's deadline

stem: A coordinator keeps re-delegating to close coverage gaps in one evolving report; after eleven cycles of only small wording changes it still has not stopped, and the token budget is nearly exhausted. What should determine when the loop ends?

opts.t: Split the report into independent aspects and dispatch them as a parallel fan-out from one coordinator turn.
Attribute the stall to the synthesis agent's limits and replace it with a higher-capacity model.
Define explicit sufficiency criteria for the coordinator to evaluate the synthesis against, rather than a cycle count.
Keep re-delegating as needed, and log each cycle's token spend for review once the run finishes.

whyRight: The loop's actual defect is the absence of a sufficiency criterion the coordinator can evaluate against; small wording changes each cycle show the agent still executes normally. A cycle count or budget ceiling only caps runaway spend, it does not tell the coordinator when the report is actually done.

whyWrong.A: Parallel fan-out fits independent subtasks dispatched together; this report has one thread of gap-closing where each cycle depends on the last pass's result, not several separable aspects.
whyWrong.B: Small wording changes each cycle show the agent is still producing output, not failing outright; nothing in the stated evidence points to a capability limit, only a missing stopping rule.
whyWrong.D: Logging spend after the run only records that the budget was consumed; it supplies no criterion that stops the loop earlier, so the pattern repeats next time.

t1Clause: keeps re-delegating to close coverage gaps in one evolving report

stem: A 60-person claims team processes very high volumes of routine claims and a small share of unusually complex ones; leadership names cost per claim as the priority, and no claim carries an irreversible action once submitted. Which decomposition technique fits?

opts.t: A confidence-tier split: a cheap path for routine claims and a costlier path reserved for the complex share.
A risk-tier split: autonomous handling for reversible claims and a gated review path for any irreversible action.
Route every claim through one undifferentiated evaluation regardless of complexity, to keep the design simple.
A confidence-tier split for routine claims only, leaving complex claims in the same undifferentiated path as before.

whyRight: Leadership named cost as the priority and the population splits cleanly into a large routine share and a small hard share; a confidence-tier split lets the routine majority run the cheapest adequate path while the harder cases absorb the more expensive one.

whyWrong.B: Risk-tier splits govern blast radius from irreversible actions; the scenario states no claim carries one, so this technique answers a question the stem does not ask.
whyWrong.C: A single undifferentiated path abandons the cost lever entirely; the routine majority pays the same processing cost as the genuinely complex share.
whyWrong.D: Splitting off only the routine share leaves the complex share on the same costly path it started on, moving cost only partway toward the stated priority.

t1Clause: no claim carries an irreversible action once submitted

stem: A customer-support triage pipeline runs at very high volume, and this quarter's stated priority is cost per resolved ticket; most tickets are straightforward, and a minority need deeper investigation. Which architectural lever most directly moves the named pillar?

opts.t: Parallelise every step and precompute enrichment at ingest, ahead of when each ticket actually needs it.
Confidence-tier routing: send routine tickets to the smallest model that clears the bar, reserve larger models for the minority.
Keep every ticket on the largest available model, and add a post-hoc cost review each month to catch overspend.
Reduce the number of tickets handled by routing more of them to a human queue instead of the model.

whyRight: Cost per resolved ticket is the stated pillar, and volume means the routing choice applies to nearly every ticket. Sending the large routine share to the smallest adequate model while reserving larger models for the minority is the lever that moves cost directly, rather than latency or throughput.

whyWrong.A: Parallelising and precomputing shortens latency, which is not the stated pillar here; nothing in the scenario names a latency commitment for this pipeline to meet.
whyWrong.C: Running every ticket on the largest model first spends the most on the routine majority, then a monthly review only reports the overspend after it happens.
whyWrong.D: Shifting volume to a human queue does not scale against a very-high-volume pipeline and abandons the automated routing the scenario is asking to be designed.

t1Clause: this quarter's stated priority is cost per resolved ticket
